terms.Horizontal scaling: Horizontal scaling adds nodes rather than resources per node. It is straightforward for stateless tiers, where any instance can serve any request and autoscaling can add or remove instances on CPU, request rate or queue depth. For stateful tiers it requires partitioning (sharding) or replication, which brings coordination, rebalancing and consistency trade-offs. It also improves fault tolerance: with N+1 or N+2 capacity, losing a node or an availability zone does not cause an outage. Limits come from shared dependencies, such as database connections, a central lock or a hot key, so scaling one tier often moves the bottleneck to the next. Contrast with vertical scaling, which is simpler but capped by hardware and remains a single failure domain.
terms.Load balancer: Layer 4 balancers forward TCP or UDP connections with minimal overhead and cannot see HTTP; layer 7 balancers terminate TLS, parse requests and can route by path or header, retry, split traffic for canaries and balance individual gRPC requests over long-lived HTTP/2 connections. Algorithms include round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, power of two random choices, and hashing for affinity. Health is tracked with active probes and passive outlier detection. The balancer itself must be redundant (active-passive pairs with a floating IP, DNS with several records, anycast, or a managed service). Watch for sticky sessions that skew load, retries that amplify outages, and deep health checks that eject every backend at once when a shared dependency fails.
terms.Consistent hashing: Consistent hashing places each node at many points on the ring (virtual nodes, often 100-200 per node) to even out arc sizes and to let stronger machines take more points. Lookup is a binary search over sorted ring positions, O(log V). Adding a node takes over roughly 1/(N+1) of the keys, drawn from many existing nodes when virtual nodes are used. It is used in distributed caches, Dynamo-style databases (Cassandra, Riak) and L7 balancers that need affinity. Variants: rendezvous or highest-random-weight hashing (simpler, no ring), jump consistent hash (no memory, but nodes can only be added or removed at the end), and bounded-load consistent hashing, which caps each node at, say, 1.25x the average load to tame hot spots.
terms.Cache-aside: Cache-aside keeps the cache off the write path's critical correctness: if the cache is lost, the system is slower but still correct. Its weaknesses are the cold-miss cost, application-managed invalidation, and races. The recommended order is to write the database and then delete the key; deleting first lets a concurrent reader refill the stale value. A rarer race remains (a slow reader writes an old value after the delete), bounded by a TTL, delayed double-delete, or invalidation driven by change data capture. Compare read-through (the cache library loads on a miss), write-through (writes update cache and database together) and write-back (the cache absorbs writes and flushes later). Protect popular keys against stampedes with request coalescing and TTL jitter.
terms.Cache stampede: A stampede is a positive feedback loop: misses add database load, the database slows, rebuilds take longer, and more requests pile up behind the missing key. Defenses: request coalescing or single-flight (one rebuild per key per process, or a distributed lock such as SET lock NX EX 10), stale-while-revalidate (serve the expired value while a background refresh runs), probabilistic early expiration (each reader refreshes early with probability increasing as expiry nears), TTL jitter to spread expirations, and pre-warming after deploys or cache restarts. Related problems are cache penetration (repeated lookups of nonexistent keys; cache negative results or use a Bloom filter) and cache avalanche (mass expiry or total cache loss).
terms.B-tree index: Databases use B+ trees: internal pages hold only keys and child pointers, leaves hold keys plus row references (or the rows themselves in clustered indexes such as InnoDB's primary key), and leaves are linked for range scans. A fan-out of hundreds of keys per page keeps a billion-row index only 3-4 levels deep. Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule, so put equality columns first and range columns last. Covering indexes enable index-only scans. Costs: write amplification, page splits, memory pressure and bloat over time. Planners skip an index when a filter is not selective, because random reads cost more than a sequential scan. Alternatives include hash, GIN, GiST and BRIN indexes, and LSM trees in write-heavy stores.
terms.ACID: Atomicity and durability are implemented with a write-ahead log (WAL): changes are logged and flushed before the commit is acknowledged, then replayed or undone after a crash. Isolation is implemented with locks or multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) and comes in levels: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read and serializable, each preventing more anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates, write skew). Vendors differ: PostgreSQL's repeatable read is snapshot isolation and its serializable level aborts conflicting transactions, so clients must retry. The C in ACID concerns application invariants and constraints, unlike the C in CAP, which means linearizability. Distributed transactions need two-phase commit or consensus; across microservices, sagas replace ACID with compensations.
terms.Sharding: The shard key determines everything: it should have high cardinality, spread load evenly and match the dominant query so most requests touch one shard (tenant_id in multi-tenant SaaS is a classic). Range sharding preserves order and supports scans and automatic splits, but sequential keys create hot spots; hash sharding spreads load but scatters range queries. Avoid hash % N; use many logical shards mapped onto physical nodes, consistent hashing or a directory service so rebalancing moves little data. Cross-shard joins, global secondary indexes, unique constraints and transactions become expensive. Each shard is usually replicated for availability. Because resharding is operationally heavy, exhaust vertical scaling, read replicas, caching and archiving first.
terms.CAP theorem: Formally (Gilbert and Lynch, 2002), consistency means linearizability and availability means every request to a non-failing node eventually gets a non-error response. The theorem only constrains behavior during partitions, which is why PACELC is more useful day to day: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Dynamo-style stores are typically PA/EL; consensus-based databases such as Spanner, etcd and CockroachDB are PC/EC. Many systems are tunable per operation (quorum levels, strongly consistent reads). Common misconceptions: 'pick two of three' (partitions are not optional), treating CAP consistency as ACID consistency, and assuming AP means no consistency at all, when causal or session guarantees are still possible.
terms.Dead-letter queue: SQS (maxReceiveCount with a redrive policy) and RabbitMQ (dead-letter exchanges) support DLQs natively; in Kafka they are a convention implemented by frameworks, often with tiered retry topics (retry after 1 minute, 10 minutes) before the dead-letter topic. Retry only transient errors with backoff; route permanent failures such as schema violations straight to the DLQ. Store context with each dead letter: the original topic, partition, offset, error and attempt count. A DLQ needs alerting, an owner and a redrive tool, and replayed messages must be handled idempotently. Moving messages to a retry topic breaks per-key ordering, so systems that need strict ordering may instead pause the partition or park all later messages for the same key.
terms.Circuit breaker: A breaker has three states: closed (calls pass, failures counted over a sliding window by count or time), open (calls fail immediately, often with a fallback such as cached data or a degraded feature) and half-open (a limited number of trial calls decide whether to close or reopen). Typical settings: trip at 50% failures with a minimum of 20 calls in the window, stay open 30 s. Slow calls can count as failures. It complements timeouts (bound each call), retries with backoff and jitter (handle transient errors), bulkheads (separate pools per dependency) and retry budgets. Breakers live in client libraries (Resilience4j, Polly) or service-mesh proxies through outlier detection.
terms.Idempotency key: Implementation: insert the key atomically (a unique constraint) with a 'processing' state before doing work, then store the response status and body; repeats return the stored response, and concurrent duplicates get 409 or wait. Store a fingerprint of the request body and reject reuse of the key with different parameters. Scope keys per account and expire them after a window longer than any client retry policy, often 24 hours. Payment APIs popularized the Idempotency-Key HTTP header, which is being standardized at the IETF. The same idea applies to message consumers, which dedupe by event ID. Idempotency keys protect one hop only: downstream calls need their own keys, ideally derived deterministically from the original one.
